Find the general solution to the equation x2y″+15xy′+49y=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=c1x4+c2x−4
b
y(x)=c1x−7+c2x−7ln⁡x
c
y(x)=c1x−7+c2xln⁡x
d
y(x)=c1x7+c2x7ln⁡x
e
y(x)=c1x4+c2x4ln⁡x

decision.explanation: Substituting y=x^r gives r(r-1)+15r+49=r^2+14r+49=(r+7)^2=0. The repeated root r=-7 yields y(x)=c₁x⁻⁷+c₂x⁻⁷ ln x for x>0, matching option b.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+15x{y}^{′}+49y=0,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+15x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+49{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+15\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+49{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+15\lambda +49] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+15\lambda +49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+14\lambda +49 & =0 \\ (\lambda +7)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-7.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{-7}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-7}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

Question 1

Find the general solution to the equation x2y″+15xy′+49y=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=c1x4+c2x−4
b
y(x)=c1x−7+c2x−7ln⁡x
c
y(x)=c1x−7+c2xln⁡x
d
y(x)=c1x7+c2x7ln⁡x
e
y(x)=c1x4+c2x4ln⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2+15x⋅λxλ−1+49xλ=0λ(λ−1)xλ+15λxλ+49xλ=0xλ[λ(λ−1)+15λ+49]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+15λ+49=0λ2+14λ+49=0(λ+7)2=0.

Hence, we have a double root λ=−7. Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=c1x−7+c2x−7ln⁡x.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with a Repeated Root
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+15x{y}^{′}+49y=0,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+15x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+49{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+15\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+49{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+15\lambda +49] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+15\lambda +49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+14\lambda +49 & =0 \\ (\lambda +7)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-7.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{-7}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-7}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

b

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation is r(r-1)-11r+36=(r-6)^2=0, so y=t^6(C₁+C₂ ln t). From y(1)=4, C₁=4. Since y′(1)=6C₁+C₂=0, C₂=-24. Thus y=4t^6(1-6 ln t), option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Find the solution of the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-11t{y}^{′}+36y=0,\,y(1)=4,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-11t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+36{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-11\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+36{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =6.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{6}+{c}_{2}{t}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=4$ into the general solution gives

$$
4={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6{c}_{1}{t}^{5}+{c}_{2}{t}^{5}+6{c}_{2}{t}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and ${c}_{1}=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =6{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 0 & =24+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =4{t}^{6}-24{t}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t \\  & =4{t}^{6}(1-6\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the solution of the initial value problem t2y″−11ty′+36y=0,y(1)=4,y′(1)=0,t>0.

a
y(t)=4t6(1−6ln⁡t)
b
y(t)=t6(4−ln⁡t)

EXPLANATION

The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=tλ. Differentiating y with respect to t gives

y′=λtλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)tλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

t2⋅λ(λ−1)tλ−2−11t⋅λtλ−1+36tλ=0λ(λ−1)tλ−11λtλ+36tλ=0tλ[λ(λ−1)−11λ+36]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)−11λ+36=0λ2−12λ+36=0(λ−6)2=0.

Hence, we have a double root λ=6. Therefore, the general solution is y(t)=c1t6+c2t6ln⁡t.

Now let's find the constants c1 and c2.

Substituting y(1)=4 into the general solution gives 4=c1.

We now need to apply the condition y′(1)=0. First, we differentiate y to find y′: y′=6c1t5+c2t5+6c2t5ln⁡t

Substituting y′(1)=0 and c1=4 into the above gives 0=6c1+c20=24+c2c2=−24.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(t)=4t6−24t6ln⁡t=4t6(1−6ln⁡t).

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with a Repeated Root
content.problem:
Find the solution of the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-11t{y}^{′}+36y=0,\,y(1)=4,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-11t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+36{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-11\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+36{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =6.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{6}+{c}_{2}{t}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=4$ into the general solution gives

$$
4={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6{c}_{1}{t}^{5}+{c}_{2}{t}^{5}+6{c}_{2}{t}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and ${c}_{1}=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =6{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 0 & =24+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =4{t}^{6}-24{t}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t \\  & =4{t}^{6}(1-6\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Given that the differential equation

x2y″+11xy′+25y=0

has the general solution

y=c1x−5+c2x−5ln⁡x,

solve the initial value problem

x2y″+11xy′+25y=0,y(1)=2,y′(1)=3,x>0.

a
y(x)=2+6ln⁡xx5
b
y(x)=4−3ln⁡xx5
c
y(x)=2−8ln⁡xx5
d
y(x)=3−9ln⁡xx5
e
y(x)=2+13ln⁡xx5
Submit

decision.explanation: From y=x⁻⁵(c₁+c₂ ln x), y(1)=2 gives c₁=2. Differentiating gives y′=x⁻⁶[-5c₁+c₂-5c₂ ln x], so y′(1)=3 implies -10+c₂=3 and c₂=13. Therefore option e satisfies the initial value problem.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+11x{y}^{′}+25y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{-5}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+11x{y}^{′}+25y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=2.$ Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=3.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-5{c}_{1}{x}^{-6}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-6}-5{c}_{2}{x}^{-6}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=3$ and ${c}_{1}=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =-5(2)+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =2{x}^{-5}+13{x}^{-5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =\frac{2+13\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Given that the differential equation

x2y″+11xy′+25y=0

has the general solution

y=c1x−5+c2x−5ln⁡x,

solve the initial value problem

x2y″+11xy′+25y=0,y(1)=2,y′(1)=3,x>0.

a
y(x)=2+6ln⁡xx5
b
y(x)=4−3ln⁡xx5
c
y(x)=2−8ln⁡xx5
d
y(x)=3−9ln⁡xx5
e
y(x)=2+13ln⁡xx5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We find the constants c1 and c2 using the initial conditions.

  • First, we apply the condition y(1)=2. Substituting y(1)=2 into the general solution gives 2=c1.

  • Then, we apply the condition y′(1)=3. Differentiating y, we get y′=−5c1x−6+c2x−6−5c2x−6ln⁡x.

Substituting y′(1)=3 and c1=2 into the above gives 3=−5(2)+c2c2=13.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(x)=2x−5+13x−5ln⁡x=2+13ln⁡xx5.

content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+11x{y}^{′}+25y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{-5}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+11x{y}^{′}+25y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=2.$ Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=3.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-5{c}_{1}{x}^{-6}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-6}-5{c}_{2}{x}^{-6}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=3$ and ${c}_{1}=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =-5(2)+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =2{x}^{-5}+13{x}^{-5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =\frac{2+13\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substituting y=x^r gives r(r-1)-11r+36=r²-12r+36=(r-6)²=0. The repeated root r=6 gives the general solution y=c₁x⁶+c₂x⁶ ln x for x>0, matching option b.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-11x{y}^{′}+36y=0,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-11x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+36{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-11\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+36{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =6.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{6}+{c}_{2}{x}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

Find the general solution to the equation x2y″−11xy′+36y=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=c1x−6+c2ln⁡x
b
y(x)=c1x6+c2x6ln⁡x

d

e
y(x)=c1x−4+c2x9

EXPLANATION

The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2−11x⋅λxλ−1+36xλ=0λ(λ−1)xλ−11λxλ+36xλ=0xλ[λ(λ−1)−11λ+36]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)−11λ+36=0λ2−12λ+36=0(λ−6)2=0.

Hence, we have a double root λ=6. Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=c1x6+c2x6ln⁡x.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with a Repeated Root
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-11x{y}^{′}+36y=0,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-11x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+36{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-11\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+36{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =6.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{6}+{c}_{2}{x}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+13x{y}^{′}+36y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{-6}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-6}\operatorname{ln}⁡x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+13x{y}^{′}+36y=0,\,y(1)=4,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-10,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=4.$ Substituting $y(1)=4$ into the general solution gives

$$
4={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-10.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-6{c}_{1}{x}^{-7}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-7}-6{c}_{2}{x}^{-7}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=-10$ and ${c}_{1}=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-10 & =-6(4)+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =14.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =4{x}^{-6}+14{x}^{-6}\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =\frac{4+14\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{6}}.\end{aligned}

We find the constants c1 and c2 using the initial conditions.

  • First, we apply the condition y(1)=4. Substituting y(1)=4 into the general solution gives 4=c1.

  • Then, we apply the condition y′(1)=−10. Differentiating y, we get y′=−6c1x−7+c2x−7−6c2x−7ln⁡x.

Substituting y′(1)=−10 and c1=4 into the above gives −10=−6(4)+c2c2=14.

content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+13x{y}^{′}+36y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{-6}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-6}\operatorname{ln}⁡x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+13x{y}^{′}+36y=0,\,y(1)=4,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-10,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=4.$ Substituting $y(1)=4$ into the general solution gives

$$
4={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-10.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-6{c}_{1}{x}^{-7}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-7}-6{c}_{2}{x}^{-7}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=-10$ and ${c}_{1}=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-10 & =-6(4)+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =14.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =4{x}^{-6}+14{x}^{-6}\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =\frac{4+14\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{6}}.\end{aligned}
$$
